title: Secure AI Supply Chain, Procurement, and Provenance
intro: Securing what you buy and borrow: recognising where AI vendor risk hides and reading certifications and assessment reports critically; acquiring AI with clear data ownership, licences checked along a model’s pedigree and an eye on legal and regulatory roles; verifying the pedigree and provenance of models and datasets with hashes, signatures and attestations; and maintaining AI bills of materials that cover hardware, software and data.
objectives: Identify AI-specific third-party risks, and interpret certifications, SOC 2 reports, test reports and model documentation critically
Apply AI acquisition practices covering data ownership, licensing along the pedigree, and legal and regulatory roles
Verify the pedigree and provenance of models and datasets using cryptographic hashing, digital signatures and attestations
Produce and maintain AI bills of materials covering hardware, software and data, and use them with VEX in vulnerability response

sections.title: Third-party AI vendor risk and assurance evidence

blocks.title: Reading the evidence, not the logo

scenes.title: Reading the evidence, not the logo
scenes.sub: Third-party AI vendor risks, certifications and assessment reports
scenes.say: Most organisations’ AI depends on vendors: model providers, AI features inside existing software, and agents connected to internal systems. Vendors offer certificates and reports as proof of security, but a logo proves little until you read what it covers. | This video covers third-party AI vendor risks, and how to read assessment reports critically, building on the due diligence in Module 2.5.

scenes.title: Where AI vendor risk hides

items.d: New AI in tools you already use
Many vendors, the same few models
Where data, staff and laws sit

scenes.say: AI vendor risk often hides in six places. | Embedded AI features: vendors add AI to software you already use, sometimes switched on by default, changing where your data goes without a new contract. | Fourth parties: your vendor may send your data to its own model providers, so their security becomes your risk too. | Integration tokens: AI agents and chat tools connected to your email, CRM or files hold tokens that can reach your data. | Shared foundations: many vendors use the same few foundation models, so one provider’s outage or flaw hits several suppliers at once. | Fragile suppliers: AI start-ups pivot, get acquired or shut down, and your data may move with them. | And jurisdiction: where data is processed, where support staff sit, and which laws apply.

scenes.title: When an AI vendor’s tokens are stolen

events.d: Stolen tokens for an AI chat agent’s CRM link
Exports searched for keys and passwords
Vendor and CRM platform cut the link
Exposed keys rotated; connected apps reviewed

scenes.say: Here is a real example of integration risk, from August 2025. | A threat actor used stolen OAuth tokens belonging to Salesloft Drift, an AI chat agent that customers had connected to their Salesforce CRM. | With those tokens, the actor exported large volumes of CRM data from many organisations. Google’s threat intelligence team said more than seven hundred were potentially affected. | The exported records were searched for secrets, such as cloud access keys and passwords, to reach further systems. | On the twentieth of August, the vendor revoked the connections, and the CRM platform removed the app from its marketplace. | Customers had to rotate any credentials stored in their records, and review every connected app. The lesson: scope each integration’s access tightly, monitor what it does, and keep secrets out of business records.

scenes.title: Reading a SOC 2 report
scenes.code:
Report: SOC 2 Type II, AcmeAI platform
Period: 1 Oct 2025 to 30 Sep 2026
Opinion: unmodified (no qualifications)
In scope: inference API, admin console
Not in scope: fine-tuning service (we use it)
Carved out: cloud host, model provider
Exceptions: 2 (late access reviews)
CUECs: SSO, admin review, key rotation
Bridge letter: covers to 31 Dec 2026

notes.d: The opinion page is the start, not the end.
Type II tests operation over time. Unmodified means no qualifications.
The service you actually use must be in scope.
Excluded suppliers need their own evidence.
Read management’s responses. CUECs are controls you must run.
A bridge letter is the vendor’s statement, not an audit.

scenes.say: Here are an assessor’s notes on a vendor’s SOC 2 Type Two report. Read the whole report, not just the opinion. | Type Two means controls were tested over a period, here twelve months, and an unmodified opinion means the auditor had no qualifications. | But the scope covers the inference service and console, not the fine-tuning service this customer actually uses. That gap needs other evidence. | The cloud host and the model provider are carved out, so you need their reports too. | Read the exceptions and management’s responses. And note the complementary user entity controls: controls the report assumes you run, such as single sign-on. | Finally, the bridge letter covering the months since the period ended is the vendor’s own statement, not an audit.

items: AI vendor risk hides in embedded features, fourth parties and integrations
Read each report’s scope, period, exceptions and carve-outs
Run the controls the vendor expects you to run (CUECs)
Monitor vendors and every integration’s access continuously
scenes.say: To recap. | AI vendor risk hides in embedded features, fourth parties, integrations, shared foundations, fragile suppliers and jurisdiction. | Read every report’s scope, period, exceptions and carve-outs, not just its conclusion. | Run the controls the vendor expects you to run. | And monitor vendors, and every integration’s access, continuously.

blocks.md:
### AI-specific vendor risks
| Risk | What to do |
|---|---|
| **Embedded AI features**, added to existing products and sometimes on by default | Contract for advance notice and the right to keep new AI features off; review admin settings after releases |
| **Fourth parties**: the vendor’s own model providers and sub-processors | Identify them and their regions; obtain their assurance; flow terms down |
| **Integration and agent access**: OAuth tokens and API keys for email, CRM, files and code | Inventory connected apps; least-privilege scopes; monitor API activity; revoke unused tokens; keep secrets out of records |
| **Shared foundations**: many vendors on the same few models and clouds | Map dependencies; plan for correlated outages and flaws (Module 5.7) |
| **Fragile suppliers** that pivot, are acquired or close | Check financial health; contract for data return, deletion and transition |

### Reading assurance evidence
| Evidence | What it shows | What to check |
|---|---|---|
| **SOC 2 Type II** | Controls, against the AICPA Trust Services Criteria, operated effectively over a period, typically 6 to 12 months. **Type I** covers design at a point in time only | Scope (system description); opinion (unmodified or modified); exceptions and responses; **carved-out** subservice organisations; **CUECs**; any **bridge letter**, which is unaudited |
| **ISO/IEC 27001 or 42001 certificate** | An audited management system | Scope statement; an **accredited** certification body (**ISO/IEC 42006**, July 2025, adds requirements for bodies certifying 42001); validity within the three-year cycle; the 27001 Statement of Applicability |
| **CSA STAR for AI** (October 2025) | **Level 1**: the vendor’s self-assessment against the AI Controls Matrix (Module 2.5). **Level 2**: independent assurance based on ISO/IEC 42001 | Which level; self-assessments aren’t verified |
| **Pen test and AI red-team reports** | Weaknesses found at one point in time | Date and version tested; whether prompts, tools, agents and data leakage were in scope (for example, mapped to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications or MITRE ATLAS); severity, remediation and retest; tester independence. A one-page attestation letter isn’t a report |
| **Model and system cards** | The vendor’s own evaluations, intended use and limitations | Coverage; confirm what matters with your own tests (Module 6.4). Under the EU AI Act, providers of general-purpose AI models must give integrators documentation (Section 2) |

Certification shows that a managed system exists; it doesn’t prove that a particular model is secure. **Trust centres** make documents easier to obtain, often under an NDA, but don’t change what they show.

### Tiering and continuous monitoring
Set assessment depth by **tier** (Module 2.3): data sensitivity, the access and autonomy granted, criticality and regulatory exposure. Between reviews, watch for certificate expiry and new report periods, sub-processor and fourth-party changes, new AI features and model deprecations, breach disclosures and advisories, and **integration activity** such as unusual API volumes, new scopes and unused tokens.

blocks.title: The well-certified assistant
blocks.md: A bank is assessing an AI assistant that will connect to its CRM and email. The vendor’s trust centre shows an ISO/IEC 42001 certificate, a SOC 2 Type II report and a “clean” penetration test letter. On reading them, the security team finds that the 42001 scope covers only the vendor’s research division, the SOC 2 report carves out the model provider, and the test letter is 20 months old, from before the email integration existed.

q.q: What is the BEST next step?
o: Accept the evidence, since three independent sources together outweigh the gaps in each
Close each gap: model provider reports, current AI testing and in-scope certification
Reject the vendor outright, since any gap in assurance shows a dishonest supplier
Ask the vendor to sign a statement confirming its controls also cover the assistant
q.why: Each document has a gap that matters for this use: the wrong certificate scope, a carved-out model provider and a stale test that misses the email integration. Close those gaps with in-scope evidence, or with compensating controls and contract terms. Accepting ignores the gaps, rejecting is disproportionate, and a signed statement adds no independent assurance.

blocks.title: Assurance evidence questions
blocks.md: The best answer **reads the evidence**: the right **scope**, **period** and **service**, **independent** where it matters, and **current** for the AI features in use. A logo, a self-assessment or a bridge letter is weaker than an in-scope Type II report or a recent, AI-specific test. For integrations, think **least-privilege tokens and monitoring**.

q.q: An AI vendor’s SOC 2 Type II report lists complementary user entity controls, including enforcing single sign-on and reviewing administrator access each quarter. What does this mean for the customer?
o: The vendor’s auditor performs these controls on the customer’s behalf each quarter
The customer must operate these controls for the report’s assurance to apply to it
These are optional suggestions that the customer can safely choose to ignore
The report is invalid until the vendor implements these controls on its own side
q.why: CUECs are controls the vendor’s control design assumes the customer operates. If the customer doesn’t run them, the assurance in the report doesn’t fully hold for that customer.

sections.title: Acquiring AI: ownership, licences and legal duties

blocks.title: Who owns it, and what may you do with it?

scenes.title: Who owns it, and what may you do with it?
scenes.sub: Acquisition, data ownership, licensing and legal considerations
scenes.say: Acquiring AI means acquiring rights as well as technology: rights over your data, outputs and customised models, and permission to use models and datasets the way you intend. Get these wrong, and a working product can become unusable overnight. | This video covers AI acquisition practices, data ownership, licensing, and the legal and regulatory considerations that shape them.

scenes.title: Data ownership in AI deals
rows: Yours, exportable, used only by you
Who sees them, for how long?
scenes.say: Start with data ownership, asset by asset. | Inputs: ask whether the vendor keeps your prompts and files, and trains on them. Aim for customer ownership, and no training without explicit consent. | Outputs: aim for customer ownership, backed by IP protection such as an indemnity. | Fine-tuned models and adapters built on your data: aim for exclusive use, and export on exit. | Logs: aim for minimal logging, agreed retention and certified deletion. | And derived data, such as embeddings and usage analytics, can reveal the source data, so treat it as your data too.

scenes.title: Licences follow the pedigree
scenes.say: Licences range from permissive ones, such as Apache 2.0, to community licences with usage policies and user thresholds, responsible AI licences with use restrictions, and non-commercial terms. And obligations build up along a model’s pedigree. Here, a team starts from an open-weight base model under a community licence. | It fine-tunes the model for a specialist task. | But the tuning dataset is licensed for non-commercial use only, and its terms may now restrict the fine-tuned model too. | Someone publishes a quantised copy for easier deployment, without the licence files. | Another team builds a paid product on that copy, believing it to be unrestricted. | A licence review traces the pedigree, finds the non-commercial restriction and the base model’s usage policy, and stops the launch until both are resolved. Remember, too, that open weights aren’t open source.

scenes.title: Legal and regulatory checkpoints

items.d: Rebranding or modifying can make you the provider

scenes.say: Six legal and regulatory checkpoints shape AI acquisition. | Your EU AI Act role. Rebranding, substantially modifying or repurposing a high-risk system can make you its provider. | Upstream documentation. Providers of general-purpose AI models must inform the providers who integrate them, so ask for it. | Data protection: controller and processor roles, processing agreements, international transfers and impact assessments. | Sector rules. For example, the EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act sets contract terms for financial entities’ ICT providers. | Public sector rules. For example, US federal guidance from April 2025 bars agency AI vendors from training on non-public agency data without consent. | And export controls and sanctions, covering advanced chips, some model technology and restricted parties.

items: Settle ownership of inputs, outputs, fine-tunes, logs and derived data
Check every licence along the pedigree, verified at source
Know your regulatory role; get upstream documentation
Check data protection, sector, public sector and export rules
scenes.say: To recap. | Settle ownership of inputs, outputs, fine-tunes, logs and derived data in the contract. | Check every licence along a model’s pedigree, verified at source. | Know your role under AI regulation, and get documentation from upstream providers. | And check data protection, sector, public sector and export rules before you commit.

blocks.md:
### AI acquisition practices
Building on the due diligence and contract terms in Module 2.5:
- **Match depth to the use case’s tier** (Module 2.3), and **pilot** with synthetic or non-sensitive data.
- **Control feature creep:** require advance notice of new AI features in products you already use, with the right to keep them off.
- **Plan for portability:** open formats, exportable fine-tunes, documented prompts and evaluation sets, and transition help.
- **Keep testing rights** (Module 6.4) and **version pinning with deprecation notice** (Module 6.2), and **close out cleanly** with data return, certified deletion and revoked tokens.

### Data ownership
| Asset | Position to seek |
|---|---|
| **Inputs** (prompts, files) | Customer-owned; no training or product improvement without explicit consent; retention limits, or zero retention |
| **Outputs** | Customer-owned as far as the law allows; an IP indemnity whose conditions you understand (Module 2.4) |
| **Fine-tunes and adapters** | Exclusive use; exportable in a usable format; deleted on request |
| **Logs and monitoring data** | Defined purpose, retention and access; available to you for investigations |
| **Derived data** (embeddings, analytics) | Treated as customer data, because it can reveal the source |

### Licensing
| Type | Examples | Typical conditions |
|---|---|---|
| **Permissive** | Apache 2.0, MIT, CC BY | Keep notices; give attribution |
| **Community** | Several open-weight model families | Acceptable use policy; naming or attribution rules; a separate licence above a user threshold (700 million monthly active users in Meta’s Llama licences) |
| **Responsible AI (RAIL)** | OpenRAIL-M | Prohibited uses that must flow down to recipients |
| **Non-commercial** | CC BY-NC, research licences | No commercial use |
| **Share-alike** | CC BY-SA, copyleft licences | Derivatives under the same terms |
| **Provider terms** | Hosted model APIs | Limits such as no training of competing models on outputs |

- **Open weights aren’t open source.** The OSI’s **Open Source AI Definition 1.0** (October 2024) also requires the code and detailed information about the training data.
- **Licences follow the pedigree:** a fine-tune, merge or copy may carry the obligations of every parent and dataset. Record them in the AIBOM (Section 4).
- **Verify at source.** The Data Provenance Initiative’s audit of more than 1,800 text datasets (2024) found over 70% of licences on popular hosting sites unspecified, and about half of those given wrong, often more permissive than the original.

### Legal and regulatory considerations
| Area | Consideration |
|---|---|
| **EU AI Act** | **Article 25**: rebranding, substantially modifying or repurposing a system into high risk makes you its **provider**. **Article 53**: providers of general-purpose AI models must document capabilities and limitations for integrators, and publish a summary of training content |
| **Data protection** | Controller and processor roles; GDPR Article 28 agreements; transfer mechanisms; DPIAs (Module 3.1) |
| **Financial services** | **DORA** (applying since January 2025): a register of ICT arrangements, mandatory contract terms and exit strategies; the first critical ICT third-party providers were designated in November 2025 |
| **US federal** | **OMB M-25-22** (April 2025): contracts must set out IP rights, **permanently prohibit** training on non-public agency data without consent, and address portability |
| **Export controls** | Advanced chips, some model technology, restricted parties |

blocks.title: The model that looked free
blocks.md: A retailer’s data science team found a fine-tuned model on a public hub that answers product questions well. Its model card says it was tuned from a popular open-weight base model “using publicly available datasets”, and the hub lists its licence as Apache 2.0. The team wants to use it in a paid, customer-facing service next month.

q.q: What should happen BEFORE the model is approved for commercial use?
o: Nothing more, because the hub lists the model under the permissive Apache 2.0 licence
Trace the pedigree: the base model’s licence and policy, and dataset licences at source
Rename the model in the product so that it can’t easily be linked back to its origin
Restrict it to internal staff, so that the licence conditions no longer apply to it
q.why: A hub label is weak evidence, and a fine-tune may carry the obligations of its base model and its tuning data. Tracing the pedigree and verifying licences at source is the right step. Renaming would hide a possible breach, and internal use doesn’t make licence terms disappear.

blocks.title: Acquisition questions
blocks.md: Look for answers that **settle rights before use**: customer ownership of inputs, outputs and fine-tunes; **no training on your data without consent**; **licence checks along the pedigree**, verified at source; and awareness of **role changes** under the EU AI Act. "It’s free to download" and "the hub says Apache 2.0" are traps.

q.q: A company puts its own brand on a third-party high-risk AI system and sells it to customers in the EU. What is the MOST significant regulatory consequence?
o: The original provider’s obligations transfer automatically to the company’s customers
The company may take on all the provider’s obligations for the high-risk system
The system is reclassified as minimal risk once a distributor has rebranded it
The company only needs to update the marketing materials that describe the system
q.why: Under Article 25 of the EU AI Act, putting your name or trademark on a high-risk system can make you its provider, with the full set of provider obligations. Obligations don’t pass to customers, rebranding doesn’t change the risk class, and marketing changes aren’t enough.

blocks.title: Where did this model really come from?

scenes.title: Where did this model really come from?
scenes.say: A model file tells you almost nothing about its history. It could be an official release, a community fine-tune, a merge of two models, or an altered copy, and each step brings its own data and intentions into your system. | This video covers pedigree and provenance verification with hashes, signatures and attestations, building on the artefact checks in Modules 3.6 and 3.7.

scenes.title: A model’s pedigree
scenes.say: Pedigree is a model’s family tree. It often starts with a base model, released and signed by a lab. | The lab may publish an instruction-tuned version. So far, the history is clear. | Then a community member fine-tunes it on undisclosed data, and you inherit whatever that data contained. | Someone merges that fine-tune with another model, adding a second parent to verify. | Another person quantises the merged model and re-uploads it. | And that copy is what your team wants to deploy. Which of these steps can you verify, and which are you taking on trust?

scenes.title: Pedigree and provenance
rows: Where did this exact file come from?
Inherited flaws and licences go unseen
scenes.say: Pedigree and provenance answer different questions. | Pedigree asks what a model descends from: its parents, the data and methods at each step, and who carried them out. Provenance asks where this exact file came from, and how it was produced. | Pedigree evidence is lineage records linked to each parent’s hash. Provenance evidence is hashes, signatures and build attestations. | Without pedigree, inherited backdoors, data problems and licences go unseen. Without provenance, substituted or tampered files go unseen.

scenes.title: A verification record
scenes.code:
artefact: support-base-8b @ rev 3f9c2e1
files: 14, every SHA-256 digest matches
signature: valid (OpenSSF model signing)
signer: release-pipeline@vendor.example
transparency log: entry found
provenance: vendor CI, source tag v2.1
parent: base-8b, digest matches approved
datasets: 3 listed, 1 licence unverified
format: safetensors, no executable code
decision: HOLD until dataset licence clears

notes.d: Every check, its result and the decision.
Pinned to an immutable revision; every file hashed.
A valid signature from the expected identity, logged publicly.
Built by the expected pipeline, from a verified parent.
An unverified dataset licence; a safe file format.
Any open question holds the model back.

scenes.say: Here is a verification record for a third-party model: every check, its result and the decision. | Identity and integrity: the model is pinned to an immutable revision, and every file’s digest matches the publisher’s manifest. | Authenticity: the signature is valid, it comes from the identity the vendor told us to expect, and it is recorded in a public transparency log. | Provenance and pedigree: an attestation shows the vendor’s pipeline built the model from a tagged source, and the parent’s digest matches the version we approved. | Data and format: one tuning dataset’s licence is unverified, and the weights are in a safe format. | So the model is held. Verification fails closed. And remember its limits: a signature proves who signed, not that a model is safe, so verification always goes with your own evaluation.

items: Pedigree: what it descends from; provenance: where this file came from
Hash every file; verify signatures, attestations and parents
Record results, and fail closed on open questions
Signed isn’t safe: pair verification with evaluation
scenes.say: To recap. | Pedigree is what a model descends from; provenance is where this exact file came from, and how it was made. | Hash every file, verify signatures and attestations, and check each parent against approved digests. | Record every result, and fail closed while any question is open. | And remember that signed isn’t safe: pair verification with your own evaluation, and keep monitoring.

blocks.md:
### Pedigree and provenance
- **Pedigree** is the lineage of a model or dataset: its ancestors, the derivation steps between them (pre-training, instruction tuning, fine-tuning, merging, distillation, quantisation), the data and methods used, and who performed each step. CycloneDX records it in **pedigree** fields for ancestors, descendants, variants and patches.
- **Provenance** is the verifiable record of where a specific artefact came from and how it was produced, bound to its digest (Module 3.7).
- Hub lineage, such as a base model field in a model card, is **self-declared**: useful for discovery, but anyone can write it.

**Why pedigree matters:** descendants can inherit **backdoors** that persist through further training (Module 3.3); **weakened safety**, because fine-tuning can erode a parent’s safety training (Module 1.2); **data problems**, such as personal or poisoned data; every parent’s **licence obligations** (Section 2); and **vulnerable** loading code or file formats.

### Verification techniques
| Technique | Verifies | Practice |
|---|---|---|
| **Cryptographic hashing** | The bytes match a trusted reference | SHA-256 digests for every file, in a signed manifest; pin hub models to an immutable **revision**, never a name or default branch (Module 3.6) |
| **Digital signatures** | Who signed, and that nothing has changed since | **OpenSSF Model Signing** (v1.0, April 2025) signs whole model directories and supports **Sigstore** keyless signing with a public transparency log. Verify against the **expected identity**, not just any valid signature |
| **Provenance attestations** | How and where it was built | Signed **SLSA** provenance and **in-toto** attestations, bound to the digest (Module 4.3) |
| **Pedigree records** | What it descends from | Lineage in the AIBOM and model card, with each parent’s digest and, ideally, a signed attestation for each derivation step |
| **Dataset and content provenance** | Where data came from, and on what terms | Dataset metadata such as MLCommons **Croissant**; **C2PA** content credentials for media (Module 2.6) |

### Chain of custody
Record an artefact’s digest when it enters the organisation, and verify it at **every** hand-off: scanning, evaluation, approval, mirroring, deployment and model load. After approval, **counter-sign** it with your own identity, so admission control trusts a single internal signer (Module 4.3).

| Source | Minimum before production |
|---|---|
| **Your own pipelines** | Pipeline-identity signature, attestation, AIBOM |
| **Contracted vendors** | Vendor signature and attestation, AIBOM, notice of changes |
| **Major labs on public hubs** | Verified organisation, pinned revision, signature where offered, scanning, your own evaluation, internal mirror |
| **Unknown publishers** | Sandbox only, until pedigree, data and licences are verified |

**Verification has limits.** Signed isn’t safe, attested isn’t honest, claimed lineage isn’t proven, a clean scan can’t see behaviours hidden in the weights, popularity can be gamed, and today’s verification can be undone by tomorrow’s revocation or account takeover.

blocks.title: Verifying a claimed pedigree
items: Collect the claims
Gather the model card, hub metadata and any AIBOM entries for every claimed parent, dataset and derivation step.
Verify the parents
Match each parent’s digest to its official, signed release. An unmatched parent is an unverified link.
Check each step
Look for signed attestations for each fine-tune, merge or conversion, or reproduce the step yourself from the verified parent.
Reconcile data and licences
Confirm datasets and licences at source, and combine every parent’s obligations.
Test, record and decide
Evaluate behaviour yourself, record the results in the AIBOM and registry, fail closed on gaps, and counter-sign approved artefacts.

blocks.title: Pedigree and provenance questions
blocks.md: **Hashes** prove the bytes match a trusted reference; **signatures** add who signed; **attestations** add how it was built; **pedigree records** add what it descends from. None of them proves a model is **safe**. Strong answers **pin by digest or revision**, verify against the **expected identity**, **fail closed**, and combine verification with **independent evaluation**.

q.q: A team confirms that a fine-tuned model’s signature is valid and that its files match the publisher’s digests. The model card says it was fine-tuned from an approved base model. What remains UNVERIFIED?
o: Whether the files were altered at any point after the publisher signed them
Whether it really descends from the approved base model, and using what data
Whether the signature was produced using the publisher’s own signing identity
Whether the model’s files match the digests listed in the publisher’s manifest
q.why: The signature and digests establish the files’ integrity and authenticity. The lineage claim in the model card stays unverified until the parent’s digest and the fine-tuning step are backed by records or attestations, and the tuning data has been checked.

sections.title: AI bills of materials for hardware, software and data

blocks.title: A bill of materials for the whole stack

scenes.title: A bill of materials for the whole stack
scenes.sub: AIBOMs for hardware, software and data dependencies
scenes.say: When an advisory lands, about a poisoned dataset, a flawed library or a GPU vulnerability, the first question is: are we affected, and where? An AI bill of materials answers it in minutes, if it covers the whole stack and stays accurate. | This video covers AIBOMs for hardware, software and data dependencies, building on Module 2.5.

scenes.title: What a full AIBOM covers
scenes.intro: Five layers, each with its own dependencies and its own advisories.

layers.label: Services
layers.sub: model APIs, embedding services, tool servers

layers.label: Data
layers.sub: training, tuning, evaluation and retrieval sets

ann.d: Provider, model version, region and terms for every external call.
Identity, version, hash, source, licence and sensitivity of every dataset.
Identity, version, digest, signature, licence and parents.
Pinned versions and image digests, including tokenisers and agent frameworks.
Accelerator models, driver and firmware versions, container toolkits, and settings such as ECC.

scenes.say: A full AIBOM covers five layers, each with its own advisories. | Services: every external model API, embedding service and tool server, with its provider, version, region and terms. | Data: every training, tuning, evaluation and retrieval dataset, with its version, hash, source, licence and sensitivity, so a poisoning report can be traced to every affected model. | Models: base models and adapters, with digests, signatures, licences and pedigree, so you can find every descendant of a flawed parent. | Software: frameworks, serving engines, tokenisers and container images at pinned versions, where most advisories land. | And hardware and infrastructure: accelerators, drivers, firmware, container toolkits, and settings such as error-correcting memory. In 2025, researchers showed that GPU memory bit flips could sharply cut a model’s accuracy when error correction was off, and toolkit flaws let containers escape onto GPU hosts.

scenes.title: Inside an AIBOM
scenes.code:

  pedigree: ancestors [base-llm-8b 2.1]
- type: data
  name: tickets-ft v12   pii: true
- type: library
  name: torch, vllm, tokenizers (pinned)
- type: device
  name: gpu-80gb   driver: r5xx   ecc: on

notes.d: One per release, generated by the pipeline.
Format, version and the release it describes.
Frameworks and libraries at pinned versions.

scenes.say: Here is a simplified AIBOM excerpt in CycloneDX format, generated by the pipeline for every release. | The metadata names the format and the release it describes. | The model has its version, its digest, and a pedigree entry naming its parent. | The fine-tuning dataset has its version, and a flag showing that it contains personal data. | Libraries are listed at pinned versions. | And the hardware layer records the GPU, its driver and the error-correction setting.

scenes.title: From advisory to answer

events.d: Container escape in a GPU container toolkit
5 not affected: the vulnerable feature is off

scenes.say: Here is a complete AIBOM at work on a hardware-layer advisory. | At nine o’clock, a container escape is announced in a toolkit that lets containers use GPUs. | Twenty minutes later, a query across all AIBOMs shows fourteen clusters running the affected version. | By eleven, the platform team has issued {VEX~vex} statements, saying whether each product is actually affected. Five clusters aren’t, because the vulnerable feature is switched off. | By mid-afternoon, patching is under way, starting with shared, multi-tenant clusters. | And within days, hosted AI suppliers answer with their own {VEX~vex} statements, completing the picture.

items: Cover services, data, models, software and hardware
Generate one per release in the pipeline, and sign it
Check that what actually runs matches the AIBOM
Use VEX and supplier AIBOMs to see real exposure
scenes.say: To recap. | A full AIBOM covers services, data, models, software, and hardware and infrastructure. | Generate one for every release in the pipeline, and sign it. | Check that what actually runs matches it. | And use {VEX~vex} statements and suppliers’ AIBOMs to see your real exposure.

blocks.md:
### What to record, layer by layer
| Layer | Record | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Services** | Model APIs (provider, version, region), embedding and guardrail services, tool and MCP servers, and their terms | Trace provider incidents and retirements to dependent systems |
| **Data** | Dataset identifier, version, hash, source, collection method, licence and sensitivity | Trace poisoning, licence disputes and erasure requests to affected models (Module 3.7) |
| **Models** | Identifier, version, digest, signature, licence, model card, pedigree and evaluations | Prove what runs; find the descendants of a flawed parent (Section 3) |
| **Software** | Frameworks, serving engines, tokenisers, agent frameworks, plug-ins and image digests | Most advisories land here (Module 5.4) |
| **Hardware and infrastructure** | Accelerators, driver and firmware versions, container toolkits, ECC settings, confidential computing status | GPU flaws affect isolation and integrity: **LeftoverLocals** (2024, Module 4.2); **GPUHammer** (2025), in which Rowhammer bit flips cut model accuracy by up to 80% with ECC disabled; and container toolkit escapes such as **CVE-2024-0132** and **CVE-2025-23266** |

### Standards
- **CycloneDX** (standardised as **ECMA-424**) has supported machine-learning BOMs since version 1.5, with component types for models and data, and **pedigree** fields. Version **1.7** (October 2025) added citations recording where information came from. **SPDX 3.0** (2024) added **AI** and **Dataset** profiles.
- In 2026, the **G7 Cybersecurity Working Group** (including CISA, the NCSC, BSI and ANSSI) published voluntary **minimum elements for an SBOM for AI**, in seven clusters: **metadata**; **system level properties** (components, data flows, intended use); **models**; **dataset properties**; **infrastructure**, with a link to a **hardware bill of materials (HBOM)**; **security properties**; and **key performance indicators**.

### Keeping AIBOMs trustworthy
- **Generate, don’t write:** produce AIBOMs in the pipeline from the artefacts actually built, one per release, linked to the release manifest (Module 6.2).
- **Sign them, and keep them** with the artefact, retaining old versions for investigations.
- **Check reality against the record:** admission control confirms that deployed digests match. A hotfix that bypasses the pipeline creates **AIBOM drift**.
- **Track dynamic dependencies:** runtime downloads, plug-ins and tool servers added later, and provider models that change behind an API.
- **Protect them:** an AIBOM maps your attack surface, so share it on a need-to-know basis, or under an NDA.

### VEX and supplier AIBOMs
A **VEX** (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange) statement says whether a product is **affected**, **not affected** (with a justification), **fixed** or **under investigation**, which cuts the noise from version-matching scanners. CycloneDX, CSAF and OpenVEX support it. Ask suppliers for AIBOMs and VEX statements during procurement (Module 2.5), validate and ingest them, and match them continuously against advisories. Where hosted services share only part of the picture, record the gaps and rely on notification terms.

blocks.title: The AIBOM that was wrong
blocks.md: An advisory reports a flaw in a popular model-serving engine. The security team checks the AIBOM for its customer chatbot, which lists a patched version, and closes the ticket. A week later, an incident reveals that production was running the vulnerable version all along: during an outage, an engineer had applied a manual hotfix that rolled the engine back.

q.q: Which control would MOST likely have prevented the wrong conclusion?
o: Asking engineers to email the security team whenever they apply a manual hotfix
Pipeline-generated AIBOMs, with admission checks that deployed digests match them
Updating the AIBOM by hand once a quarter, as part of the regular inventory review
Leaving the serving engine out of the AIBOM, since it changes too often to track
q.why: An AIBOM is only trustworthy if what runs matches it. Generating AIBOMs in the pipeline and verifying deployed digests at admission would have blocked or flagged the out-of-band rollback. Emails and quarterly updates are unreliable, and leaving components out defeats the purpose.

blocks.title: AIBOM questions
blocks.md: Expect the best answer to **cover every layer**, including **hardware** (devices, drivers, firmware and settings) and **data** (versions, licences and sensitivity); to be **generated automatically** and **signed** for each release; and to be **verified against what actually runs**. Use **VEX** to separate real exposure from version matches. A hand-maintained spreadsheet is never the best answer.

q.q: A scanner flags 40 AI services because their AIBOMs list a library version with a new vulnerability. Many teams say the vulnerable function is never called. What would BEST help prioritise the response?
o: Removing the library from every AIBOM until the vulnerability is fixed upstream
VEX statements recording, with justification, which services are really affected
Patching all 40 services at once, in alphabetical order, regardless of exposure
Asking the library’s maintainers to withdraw the vulnerability advisory entirely
q.why: VEX statements record whether each product is affected, with a justification such as "vulnerable code not in the execution path", so effort goes where exposure is real. Removing entries hides risk, blanket patching ignores priority, and advisories can’t be withdrawn to suit you.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a SOC 2 Type I and a Type II report?
o: Type I covers security; Type II covers only privacy and processing integrity
Type II also tests whether the controls operated effectively over a period
Type I is written by an auditor; Type II is the vendor’s own self-assessment
Type II applies only to vendors that provide AI or ML services
quiz.why: Type I assesses control design at a point in time; Type II adds testing of operating effectiveness over a period, typically 6 to 12 months.

quiz.q: In a SOC 2 report, what does it mean when a subservice organisation is "carved out"?
o: Its controls are covered in more detail than the vendor’s own controls
Its controls are excluded, so separate evidence is needed for it
It failed the audit and was removed from the vendor’s supply chain
It is owned by the vendor, so it needs no separate assessment
quiz.why: Under the carve-out method, the subservice organisation’s controls are excluded from the report, so you need its own assurance.

quiz.q: Why is a CSA STAR for AI level 1 entry weaker evidence than an independent audit?
o: It covers physical data centre security rather than AI controls
It is the vendor’s own self-assessment, without independent checks
It expires after thirty days and is rarely renewed by vendors
It is only available to vendors that are based in the United States
quiz.why: Level 1 is a published self-assessment against the AI Controls Matrix questionnaire; level 2 adds independent assurance.

quiz.q: What does the OSI’s Open Source AI Definition require beyond published weights?
o: A commercial support contract with the model’s original developer
Access to the code and detailed information about the training data
Certification of the model under ISO/IEC 42001 by an accredited body
A guarantee that the model has never produced a harmful output
quiz.why: The 2024 definition requires the weights, the code and sufficiently detailed information about the training data. Most "open" models publish weights only.

quiz.q: Why should a model’s licence be checked along its whole pedigree?
o: Only the most recent licence in a chain of derived models is binding
Derived models may carry obligations from every parent and dataset
Model hubs merge all licences in a chain into one permissive licence
Older licences expire once a model is fine-tuned or quantised
quiz.why: Fine-tunes, merges and copies may inherit the conditions of their base models and tuning data, so obligations accumulate.

quiz.q: Which contract position BEST protects the inputs an organisation sends to an AI vendor?
o: Inputs become the vendor’s property, in exchange for a lower price
Customer ownership, no training without consent, limited retention
The vendor may use inputs to improve services if it anonymises them
The vendor decides retention according to its operational needs
quiz.why: Clear ownership, no training without explicit consent and defined retention keep the organisation in control of its data.

quiz.q: What does OMB M-25-22 require US federal AI contracts to say about non-public agency data?
o: Vendors must publish it, so that others can compete for future AI contracts
Vendors may not use it to train public or commercial AI without consent
Vendors must store it only in data centres located outside the United States
Vendors must share it with all model providers to improve government AI
quiz.why: The April 2025 memorandum requires contracts to permanently prohibit vendors from training publicly or commercially available AI on non-public agency data without explicit consent.

o: The number of downloads and likes it has received on a public hub
Its lineage: parents, derivation steps, data and who did each step
The digital signature its original publisher applied to the files
The legal entity that currently owns the copyright in its weights
quiz.why: Pedigree is the family tree: ancestors, derivation steps such as fine-tuning or merging, and the data and producers involved.

quiz.q: What does a valid digital signature on a model prove?
o: That the model contains no backdoors or hidden behaviours
Who signed it, and that it hasn’t changed since signing
That the model was trained only on lawfully obtained data
That the model performs well on standard benchmarks
quiz.why: Signatures prove authenticity and integrity, not safety, lawful data or quality.

quiz.q: Why should models from public hubs be pinned to a commit hash rather than a name?
o: Commit hashes download faster than names on most public model hubs
A name can be re-pointed or re-registered; a commit hash can’t change
Names are case-sensitive, which causes frequent download failures
Hubs charge extra fees for downloads that refer to models by name
quiz.why: Pinning to an immutable revision means a renamed, transferred or re-registered namespace can’t silently substitute a different model.

quiz.q: Which hardware details belong in an AIBOM?
o: The office floor plans and seating plans of the data science team
Accelerator models, driver and firmware versions, settings like ECC
The purchase prices and warranty dates of every GPU the firm owns
Only cloud region names, since hardware is the provider’s concern
quiz.why: Hardware flaws affect isolation and integrity, so accelerators, drivers, firmware, toolkits and security settings need recording.

o: A vendor’s marketing claim that its AI product has no vulnerabilities
A statement of whether a product is actually affected by a vulnerability
A list of every library version installed anywhere across the organisation
An emergency patch that fixes a vulnerability without needing a restart
quiz.why: VEX records whether a product is affected, not affected (with a justification), fixed or under investigation, so teams focus on real exposure.

quiz.q: Why should AIBOMs be generated by the pipeline rather than written by hand?
o: Hand-written AIBOMs are prohibited for high-risk systems under the EU AI Act
Generated AIBOMs reflect the artefacts actually built, and can be verified
Pipeline-generated AIBOMs are smaller and take up less storage space
Hand-written AIBOMs can’t record any information about datasets
quiz.why: Generating AIBOMs from the real artefacts, and signing one for each release, keeps them accurate and verifiable.

exam.q: An organisation finds that its document management vendor has added an AI summarisation feature, switched on by default, which sends files to a third-party model provider. The contract predates the feature. What should the organisation do FIRST?
o: Keep using the feature, since the vendor’s existing certifications already cover it
Switch the feature off, then assess the new data flow, fourth party and terms
Terminate the vendor contract at once and migrate all documents elsewhere
Ask staff to avoid summarising sensitive documents until the next renewal
exam.why: The feature creates a new data flow to a fourth party outside the assessed scope. Switching it off contains the exposure while the flow, provider and terms are assessed. Existing certifications may not cover it, termination is disproportionate, and relying on staff behaviour is unreliable.

exam.q: An AI vendor supplies a SOC 2 Type II report with an unmodified opinion. The report’s period ended ten months ago, and the vendor offers a bridge letter for the gap. How should the assessor treat the bridge letter?
o: As equivalent to an audit, because it extends the auditor’s opinion up to today
As management’s unaudited statement, weaker evidence than the report itself
As a sign that the vendor failed its audit, so the report should be rejected
As irrelevant, because SOC 2 reports never need to cover recent months
exam.why: A bridge letter is vendor management’s own statement about the period since the report ended. It is useful but unaudited, so weigh it accordingly and ask when the next report is due.

exam.q: An AI chat tool connected to a company’s CRM is compromised at the vendor, and attackers use its OAuth tokens to export CRM records. Which control would MOST have reduced the impact?
o: Requiring the vendor to hold an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate covering its offices
Least-privilege scopes, activity monitoring and no secrets kept in CRM records
Asking users to sign out of the chat tool at the end of every working day
Changing the CRM administrator password once a year as a routine task
exam.why: Narrow scopes limit what stolen tokens can reach, monitoring spots bulk exports, and keeping secrets out of records stops attackers pivoting further. A certificate doesn’t limit token access, and user sign-outs and annual password changes don’t affect integration tokens.

exam.q: A team wants to build a commercial product on an open-weight model released under a community licence with an acceptable use policy and a monthly active user threshold. What is the BEST approach?
o: Proceed freely, because open-weight models can be used for any purpose at all
Review the licence and policy against the use case, growth plans and obligations
Avoid all open-weight models, because their licences can’t be complied with
Rename the model in the product so that the licence terms no longer apply
exam.why: Community licences usually allow commercial use, with conditions: prohibited uses, attribution or naming rules, and a separate licence above a user threshold. Review them against the use case and expected scale.

exam.q: A bank is negotiating a contract to fine-tune a provider’s model on its own data. Which term is MOST important for avoiding lock-in?
o: A discount for committing to the provider for at least five years
Exclusive ownership of the fine-tune, exportable in a usable format
A clause letting the provider reuse the fine-tune for other customers
Monthly reports on the provider’s overall model usage statistics
exam.why: Owning the fine-tune, and being able to export it with its prompts and evaluation sets, preserves the bank’s investment if it changes provider. The other terms increase dependence or don’t address portability.

exam.q: A dataset hub lists a scraped text dataset as "CC BY 4.0", but the original source’s terms say "non-commercial research only". Which terms should guide a commercial project’s decision?
o: The hub label, because hubs verify every dataset licence before publishing
The original source’s terms, verified at source, which are more restrictive
Whichever licence is more permissive, since the user may choose either one
Neither, because data scraped from the web carries no licence obligations
exam.why: Audits have found hub licence labels are often missing or wrong, and the original licence is frequently more restrictive. Follow the terms verified at the original source, and seek legal advice where needed.

exam.q: A security team must approve a quantised model that a community member derived from a lab’s signed release. The lab’s signature doesn’t cover the quantised files. What is the BEST way to establish trust?
o: Accept it, because the lab’s signature on the original covers all its derivatives
Quantise the verified original in-house through the pipeline, and sign the result
Check that the quantised model has many downloads and positive comments
Run a malware scan, and approve the model if no malicious code is found
exam.why: Reproducing the derivation from the verified, signed original in your own pipeline gives you provenance you control. The lab’s signature doesn’t cover altered files, popularity isn’t evidence, and a clean scan can’t reveal hidden behaviours.

exam.q: A deployment pipeline checks that model signatures are valid, but not who signed them. What is the MAIN weakness?
o: Valid signatures slow deployment down, so they should be checked less often
An attacker could sign a substitute model with their own valid identity
Signatures can only be verified by the model’s original training team
Signature checks stop models from loading on GPU-based servers
exam.why: A signature means something only when checked against an expected identity or key. Accepting any valid signature lets an attacker sign a malicious model with their own credentials.

exam.q: Which practice gives the STRONGEST chain of custody for third-party models inside an organisation?
o: Downloading the latest version from the hub every time a service starts up
Digests recorded on entry and verified at each step; counter-signing on approval
Keeping a spreadsheet of model names and the dates on which they were downloaded
Letting engineers copy approved models between servers whenever they are needed
exam.why: Verifying the same digest at every hand-off, and counter-signing approved artefacts, lets admission control trust one internal identity. The other options allow substitution or lose track of what runs.

exam.q: A public dataset is reported to be poisoned. Which AIBOM content lets the organisation MOST quickly find every affected model, including fine-tunes of affected models?
o: The names of the data scientists who trained each affected model
Dataset identifiers and versions per model, plus pedigree links
GPU driver versions and firmware settings for each training cluster
The licence terms of every serving library used by the platform
exam.why: Dataset entries show which models trained on the poisoned data, and pedigree links reveal descendants that inherited it. People, drivers and library licences don’t answer the question.

exam.q: A GPU container toolkit vulnerability allows container escape on shared clusters. The organisation’s AIBOMs record models, data and libraries, but not infrastructure. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Stop using containers for AI workloads, and run every model on bare-metal servers
Record drivers, toolkits, firmware and settings in AIBOMs, generated automatically
Ask the cloud provider to confirm in writing that its GPUs are always kept secure
Record infrastructure details, but only for clusters that host high-risk models
exam.why: Recording infrastructure dependencies automatically lets infrastructure advisories be matched as quickly as software ones. Abandoning containers is disproportionate, written assurances don’t locate exposure, and partial records leave gaps.
